items.followUp: State two differences between liquids and gases.

rubric.why: A solid has a definite shape, unlike a gas.
rubric.description: Compare the shapes of solids and gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a solid has a definite shape and a gas does not have a fixed shape.

rubric.why: A solid has a definite volume, while a gas expands to fill its container.
rubric.description: Compare the volumes of solids and gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a solid has a definite volume and a gas does not.

modelAnswer: A solid has a definite shape, whereas a gas has no fixed shape and takes the shape of its container.
A solid has a definite volume, whereas a gas expands to fill the whole container.

items.followUp: Why is the third ionization energy of magnesium higher than its second ionization energy?

rubric.why: The second electron is removed from an already positively charged magnesium ion.
rubric.description: Identify the ion from which the second electron is removed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the second ionization removes an electron from Mg+.

rubric.why: The increased positive charge holds the remaining electrons more strongly.
rubric.description: Explain why the second electron is harder to remove.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the increased positive charge of Mg+ with a stronger attraction for its electrons.

modelAnswer: The first ionization removes one electron from Mg to form Mg+; the second removes an electron from this positively charged ion.
The remaining electrons are attracted more strongly by the nucleus in Mg+, so more energy is needed to remove the second electron.

items.followUp: Give two examples of a gas-solid solution.

rubric.why: Mercury dissolved in sodium is an example of a liquid-solid solution.
rubric.description: Give one valid example of a liquid-solid solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mercury dissolved in sodium.

rubric.why: Mercury dissolved in silver or gold forms an amalgam, another liquid-solid solution.
rubric.description: Give a second valid example of a liquid-solid solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mercury dissolved in silver or gold.

modelAnswer: Mercury dissolved in sodium (a sodium amalgam).
Mercury dissolved in silver (a silver amalgam).

items.followUp: Give two examples of a solid-liquid solution.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide dissolved in water is a gas-liquid solution.
rubric.description: Give one valid example of a gas-liquid solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for carbon dioxide dissolved in water, such as soda water.

rubric.why: Oxygen dissolved in water is another gas-liquid solution.
rubric.description: Give a second valid example of a gas-liquid solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for oxygen dissolved in water.

modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide dissolved in water (soda water).
Oxygen dissolved in water.

items.followUp: Define a dilute solution and give an example.

rubric.why: A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute compared with the solvent.
rubric.description: Define a concentrated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains a relatively large amount of solute in a given amount of solvent.

rubric.why: A named concentrated solution demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: Give a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as concentrated sugar solution, concentrated salt solution, or concentrated acid.

modelAnswer: A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent.
A concentrated sugar solution is an example.

items.followUp: Define a colloid and give an example.

rubric.why: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture with undissolved particles dispersed through a fluid.
rubric.description: Define a suspension.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing insoluble particles dispersed in a liquid; noting that they settle on standing is also acceptable.

rubric.why: These are common examples of suspensions.
rubric.description: Give a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as muddy water, chalk in water, or sand in water.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which insoluble solid particles are dispersed in a liquid and settle on standing.
Muddy water is an example.

items.followUp: Write down any three characteristics of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Canal rays consist of positively charged particles.
rubric.description: State the charge or nature of canal rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying canal rays as positively charged or as streams of positive ions.

rubric.why: Canal rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.description: State their path of travel.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that canal rays travel in straight lines.

rubric.why: Their positive charge causes them to deflect toward the negative plate in an electric field.
rubric.description: State their behaviour in an electric or magnetic field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their deflection due to their positive charge, such as toward the negative plate.

rubric.why: Canal rays pass through openings in the cathode, and their properties depend on the gas in the discharge tube.
rubric.description: Give two further characteristics of canal rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they pass through perforations in the cathode and 1 mark for stating that their charge-to-mass ratio or the nature of their particles depends on the gas used.

modelAnswer: Canal rays are streams of positively charged particles (positive ions).
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields toward the negative plate.
They pass through the holes or perforations in the cathode.
Their particles and charge-to-mass ratio depend on the gas present in the discharge tube.

items.followUp: Compare an atom with a molecule.

rubric.why: A molecular ion is a group of bonded atoms carrying a net charge.
rubric.description: State what a molecular ion is.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a molecular ion as a bonded group of atoms with a net charge.

rubric.why: A molecule is electrically neutral overall.
rubric.description: State the charge of a molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a molecule has no net charge.

rubric.why: A molecular ion forms when a molecule or group of atoms gains or loses electrons.
rubric.description: Compare how a molecular ion obtains its charge with a molecule's neutrality.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the molecular ion's charge to gaining or losing electrons.

rubric.why: Examples show the distinction between a charged molecular ion and a neutral molecule.
rubric.description: Give an appropriate example of a molecular ion or molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example, such as NH4+ or SO4 2- as a molecular ion, or O2, H2O, or CO2 as a molecule.

modelAnswer: A molecular ion is a group of atoms bonded together that carries a net positive or negative charge; for example, NH4+.
A molecule is a group of atoms bonded together that is electrically neutral; for example, H2O.
A molecular ion acquires its charge by gaining or losing electrons, whereas a molecule has no net charge.
